meaning: (I saw / found that) …: reports something the speaker witnessed or experienced first-hand
nuance: The retrospective -더- reports a past perception as it struck the speaker at the time, so the source must be first-hand (seen, heard, felt, tasted). The 해요체 form is -더라고요; -더라요 is nonstandard. With the speaker's own deliberate actions it is rare (어제 나는 공부하더라 sounds odd), but it is fine for your own feelings or for reactions you observed in yourself (나도 모르게 눈물이 나더라). Past -았/었더라 reports a state already completed when you got there (가 보니 다 팔렸더라). As a question, -더라? is the speaker searching memory (이름이 뭐더라?). See also HowtoStudyKorean Lesson 118.

contrasts.note: -나 보다 infers from clues; -더라 reports what you actually saw.
-던가 asks (often yourself) to recall; -더라 states what you observed.
-더니 links an observation to a following clause; -더라 ends the sentence with it.

examples.ko: 새로 생긴 카페에 가 봤는데 커피가 진짜 맛있더라고요.
examples.en: I tried the new café, and the coffee was really good.

examples.ko: 가 보니까 표가 벌써 다 팔렸더라.
examples.en: When I got there, the tickets were already sold out.

cloze.sentence: 새로 생긴 카페에 가 봤는데 커피가 진짜 {{}}.
cloze.en: I tried the new café, and the coffee was really good.

nearMiss.hint: In 해요체 it's -더라고요: 맛있더라고요.

cloze.en: When I got there, the tickets were already sold out.

nearMiss.hint: They were already gone when you arrived: completed state, 팔렸더라고요.

cloze.sentence: 그 사람 알고 보니 내 고등학교 {{}}.
cloze.en: Turns out he was a junior from my high school.
Watching the movie, I found myself tearing up.
It was much colder up the mountain than I expected.
When I asked, it turned out he was the owner of this building.

nearMiss.hint: After a consonant, keep 이: 주인이더라고요.

cloze.sentence: 그 식당은 밤 열두 시까지 문을 {{}}.
cloze.en: That restaurant was open until midnight.

cloze.sentence: 그 영화 제목이 {{}}? 기억이 안 나네.
cloze.en: What was the name of that movie again? I can't remember.

nuance.situation: 친구가 "그 식당 어때?"라고 물어요. 당신은 거기서 직접 먹어 봤어요. (You ate there yourself.)

options.why: You saw it yourself, so -더라 reports a first-hand observation.
-나 보다 is an inference from clues, but you ate there and know.
-더라요 is nonstandard; in 해요체 say -더라고요.

nuance.situation: 어제 있었던 일을 말할 때 더 자연스러운 것은? (Which is more natural?)

options.why: -더라 reports what you observed; your own deliberate actions are rarely reported this way.

options.text: 어제 도서관에 갔는데 사람이 정말 많더라.
options.why: The crowd is something you witnessed: a typical -더라 report.

meaning: was it …? did …? (searching one's memory; also rhetorical "when did I ever …?")
nuance: Retrospective -더- plus the question ending -ㄴ가: the speaker searches memory ("Was it Tuesday?"). It is often addressed to oneself; -던가요 checks gently with others. Use -았/었던가 for an event that was already over (우리가 거기 갔던가?). Rhetorically it pushes back: 내가 언제 그런 말을 했던가? (= I never said that). In writing it also makes reflective rhetorical questions (…아니었던가). Spelling trap: -던가 (recall) vs -든가 (choice: 가든가 말든가). See also HowtoStudyKorean Lesson 117.

contrasts.note: -더라 states what you observed (and -더라? also recalls: 뭐더라?); -던가 is a recall question.
-든가/-든지 offer alternatives; -던가 recalls the past.

examples.ko: 회의가 화요일이던가? 수요일이었나?
examples.en: Was the meeting on Tuesday? Or was it Wednesday?

examples.ko: 제가 언제 그런 약속을 했던가요?
examples.en: When did I ever make such a promise?

cloze.en: Was the meeting Tuesday? Or Wednesday?

nearMiss.hint: -든가 lists choices; to search your memory use -던가: 화요일이던가.

cloze.en: Did I tell you about that?

nearMiss.hint: Spelling: recall is -던가, not -든가.

cloze.sentence: 그 사람 원래 이렇게 {{}}? 오늘따라 왜 이러지.
cloze.en: Was he always this touchy? What's with him today?
Sir, when was the deadline for this assignment again?

cloze.sentence: 제가 언제 그런 약속을 {{}}? 기억에 없는데요.
cloze.en: When did I ever make that promise? I don't remember it.

nearMiss.hint: Spelling: the recall/rhetorical question is -던가요.

cloze.sentence: 우리 처음 만난 게 몇 년 {{}}?
cloze.en: How many years ago did we first meet?
Was that shop open on Sundays too?
Was this not the very moment we had dreamed of for so long?

nuance.situation: 친구 생일이 언제인지 확실하지 않아요. 혼잣말로? (Unsure of a friend's birthday, you ask yourself.)

options.why: -던가 searches your memory.
-든가 offers alternatives ("either …or"); it can't ask yourself to recall.
-더니 links an observation to a following clause; it doesn't form a recall question.

nuance.situation: 상대가 "네가 그렇게 말했잖아"라고 해요. 당신은 그런 말을 한 적이 없다고 생각해요. (You don't think you ever said it.)

options.why: Rhetorical -던가 pushes back: "When did I ever say that?"

options.text: 내가 언제 그런 말을 했나 봐?
options.why: -나 보다 infers from evidence; it can't form a rhetorical challenge.

meaning: that (someone) was …-ing / used to …; that was … (retrospective modifier: unfinished, habitual, or closed-off past)
nuance: Compare three modifiers on 읽다: 읽은 책 (finished it), 읽던 책 (was reading it, interrupted or still in progress), 읽었던 책 (read it at some point, now recalled as past). For past habits, 자주 가던 식당 and 자주 갔던 식당 are both "the restaurant I used to go to". A one-off past event takes -았/었던 (or -(으)ㄴ), not -던. For adjectives and 이다, -던 and -았/었던 are close; -았/었던 stresses that the state is over. 먹던 밥 is leftover food someone had started. See also HowtoStudyKorean Lesson 117.

contrasts.note: -았/었었다 marks a closed-off past at the end of a sentence; -았/었던 does it inside a noun phrase.
Both carry retrospective -더-: -더라 ends a sentence, -던 modifies a noun.

examples.ko: 누가 내가 마시던 커피를 버렸어?
examples.en: Who threw out the coffee I was drinking?

examples.ko: 한때 마을의 중심이었던 시장은 이제 폐허가 되었다.
examples.en: The market that was once the heart of the village is now in ruins.

cloze.en: Who threw out the coffee I was drinking?

nearMiss.hint: 마신 커피 = coffee you finished. It's the half-drunk cup, so 마시던.
마셨던 suggests coffee you drank at some point in the past; the half-finished cup is 마시던.

cloze.en: This is where we first met.

nearMiss.hint: -던 implies an ongoing or repeated meeting; a one-time first meeting is 만났던 (or 만난).

cloze.en: The playground where I used to play as a kid is gone, apparently.

nearMiss.hint: 논 놀이터 sounds like a single finished event; a past habit is 놀던.

cloze.sentence: 그렇게 말이 {{}} 사람이 왜 갑자기 조용해졌지?
cloze.en: Why has someone who used to talk so much suddenly gone quiet?
Back when I was a college student, I stayed up every night.

nearMiss.hint: After a consonant, keep 이: 대학생이던.

cloze.en: I'll finish the novel I was reading before bed.

nearMiss.hint: You haven't finished it yet: 읽던 소설.

cloze.en: Weather that had been so cold warmed up overnight.

cloze.sentence: 한때 마을의 {{}} 시장은 이제 폐허가 되었다.
cloze.en: The market that was once the heart of the village is now in ruins.

nuance.situation: 식탁 위에 반쯤 먹은 빵이 있어요. 동생에게 "그거 내가 먹고 있던 거야"라고 하려면? (Half-eaten bread on the table.)

options.why: -던 = you had started it and weren't done.
먹은 빵 is bread you already ate; it can't be sitting there half-eaten.
먹을 빵 is bread you're going to eat; it misses that you'd already started.

nuance.situation: 10년 전 여행에서 딱 한 번 묵은 호텔을 다시 찾아갔어요. (A hotel you stayed at once, ten years ago.)

options.text: 10년 전에 묵었던 호텔에 다시 가 봤어요.
options.why: A single closed-off past stay: -았/었던.

options.text: 10년 전에 묵던 호텔에 다시 가 봤어요.
options.why: -던 suggests a stay that was ongoing or habitual, not one night a decade ago.

meaning: (I saw that) … and then / but now …: links something the speaker observed to a later change, contrast, or result
nuance: The speaker witnessed the first clause, usually about a third person, a thing, or the weather, and connects it to what followed: a change (아침엔 흐리더니 오후엔 갰다), a contrast (어제는 덥더니 오늘은 춥다), or a consequence (열심히 하더니 결국 합격했다). The first-clause subject is normally not the speaker; for the speaker's own action use -았/었더니. Both clauses look back on the past, so the main clause is not a command or suggestion. See also HowtoStudyKorean Lesson 119.

contrasts.note: -았/었더니 is for the speaker's own action and what they then found; -더니 is for what they watched someone or something else do.
-더라 ends the sentence with an observation; -더니 carries it into a following clause.

examples.ko: 아침에는 하늘이 맑더니 오후에 비가 쏟아졌다.
examples.en: The sky was clear in the morning, but it poured in the afternoon.

examples.ko: 동생이 매일 밤늦게까지 공부하더니 결국 1등을 했어요.
examples.en: My brother studied late every night, and in the end he came first.

cloze.en: It was clear in the morning, but it poured in the afternoon.
My brother studied late every night and ended up first.

nearMiss.hint: -았/었더니 is for your own action; for what you watched someone else do, use -더니: 공부하더니.

cloze.en: Yesterday was so hot, and today it's chilly.
Minji hesitated for a long while, then suddenly burst into tears.

cloze.sentence: 그 가게, 작년까지만 해도 {{}} 지금은 손님이 하나도 없어요.
cloze.en: Until last year that place was a hot spot, but now it has no customers at all.

nearMiss.hint: After a consonant, keep 이: 맛집이더니.

cloze.sentence: 그 아이는 한참을 {{}} 엄마 품에서 잠이 들었다.
cloze.en: The child cried for a long time, then fell asleep in his mother's arms.

cloze.sentence: 선배가 서류를 한번 쭉 {{}} 고개를 저었다.
cloze.en: My senior skimmed through the papers and shook his head.

nearMiss.hint: -았/었더니 would make you the one who skimmed; for what you watched, use -더니.

cloze.en: Stock prices rose for a while, then plunged at year-end.
The cold got a bit better, then got worse again.

nearMiss.hint: ㅅ stays before a consonant: 낫더니.

nuance.situation: 당신이 약을 먹었는데 두통이 나았어요. (You took medicine yourself, and the headache went away.)

options.why: Your own action and the result you found: -았/었더니.
-더니 reports someone else's action you watched; with your own action use -았/었더니.

nuance.situation: 오늘 아침엔 날씨가 좋았는데 지금은 비가 와요. 친구에게? (The weather changed since morning.)

options.text: 아침엔 날씨가 좋더니 지금은 비가 오네.
options.why: An observed change in the weather: -더니.

options.text: 아침엔 날씨가 좋았더니 지금은 비가 오네.
options.why: -았/었더니 is for your own action and what followed; weather you watched change takes -더니.

options.text: 아침엔 날씨가 좋더라도 지금은 비가 오네.
options.why: -더라도 concedes a hypothetical; it can't report a change you saw.

meaning: (when / after) I did …, (I found that / it turned out) …
nuance: The first-clause subject is the speaker (or "we"), and the second clause reports what the speaker then found or what happened in response: discovery (문을 열었더니 고양이가 있었다), result (운동을 했더니 살이 빠졌다), or someone's reaction (물어봤더니 모른대요). Close to -아/어 보니까 for discovery, but -아/어 보니까 frames the act as a deliberate try, while -았/었더니 also covers plain results and reactions. The main clause reports; it can't be a command or plan. See also HowtoStudyKorean Lesson 119.

contrasts.note: -더니 reports what you watched someone or something else do; -았/었더니 is your own action.
-아/어 보니(까) is discovery from a deliberate try; -았/었더니 also covers results and reactions.

examples.ko: 점원에게 물어봤더니 그 물건은 품절이래요.
examples.en: I asked the clerk, and they said it's sold out.

examples.ko: 커피를 너무 많이 마셨더니 잠이 안 와요.
examples.en: I drank too much coffee, and now I can't sleep.

cloze.en: I worked out for the first time in ages, and now I ache all over.

nearMiss.hint: It's your own action: 했더니.

cloze.en: I asked the clerk, and they said it's sold out.

cloze.sentence: 커피를 너무 많이 {{}} 잠이 안 와요.
cloze.en: I drank too much coffee, and now I can't sleep.
I told them I was fine, and they worried even more.

cloze.sentence: 밤늦게 음악을 크게 {{}} 옆집에서 항의가 들어왔다.
cloze.en: I played music loud late at night, and the neighbors complained.

nearMiss.hint: ㄷ-irregular: 들었더니.

cloze.en: I called the child's name, and he turned around.

nearMiss.hint: 르-irregular: 불렀더니.

cloze.en: I helped my grandmother a bit, and she gave me some pocket money.

nearMiss.hint: ㅂ-irregular: 도왔더니 (or 도와드렸더니).

cloze.en: I opened the window, and a cool breeze came in.

nuance.situation: 친구가 다이어트를 시작했고, 당신은 친구가 살이 빠진 걸 봤어요. (Your friend dieted; you saw the result.)

options.why: An action by someone else that you watched: -더니.
-았/었더니 normally makes the speaker the one acting, so this sounds like you started the diet.

nuance.situation: "I opened the fridge and found it empty"를 말하려면? (Your own action and discovery.)

options.why: Your action and what you found: -았/었더니.
With -더니 the opener would be someone else you watched, and the "I found" sense is lost.

options.text: 냉장고를 열었더니 우유 좀 사 와.
options.why: A command can't follow -았/었더니; its second clause reports what you found or what happened.

meaning: to think that …!; I can't believe … (surprise, dismay, or admiration at a fact)
nuance: Reacts to a fact the speaker finds hard to believe or remarkable. In this use, verbs take the bare stem (그런 짓을 하다니), unlike the quoted -ㄴ/는다니 (한다니 = "to hear that he does …"), which reacts to someone's words. Since surprising news usually reaches us as a report, the two overlap heavily in speech; the bare stem is the form that needs no report behind it. It can end the sentence (벌써 끝나다니!) or be followed by an evaluation (…믿을 수 없다, 대단하다, 말도 안 돼). After 이다 it becomes (이)라니: 그게 다 거짓말이라니. For adjectives the two forms coincide (비싸다니). See also HowtoStudyKorean Lesson 120.

contrasts.note: -ㄴ/는다니 echoes what someone said (그만둔다니요?); bare-stem -다니 reacts to the fact itself (그만두다니!).
-다니까 insists on what you said before; -다니 expresses surprise.

examples.ko: 그렇게 착한 사람이 그런 거짓말을 하다니 믿을 수가 없어.
examples.en: I can't believe someone so kind would tell a lie like that.

examples.ko: 그 어려운 시험에 한 번에 합격했다니 정말 대단하다.
examples.en: To pass that hard exam on the first try is really impressive.

cloze.sentence: 그렇게 착한 사람이 그런 거짓말을 {{}} 믿을 수가 없어.
cloze.en: I can't believe someone so kind would lie like that.

nearMiss.hint: Also natural if you are reacting to what you were told (the quoted -ㄴ/는다니, a separate pattern). The cue asks for the bare-stem -다니: 하다니 (or 했다니).

cloze.sentence: 벌써 한 해가 다 {{}}! 시간 진짜 빠르다.
cloze.en: The whole year is already gone! Time flies.

cloze.sentence: 이 가격에 이렇게 {{}} 말도 안 돼요.
cloze.en: This tasty at this price? It's unreal.
What a relief that the rumor was all a lie.

nearMiss.hint: After 이다, -다니 becomes -라니: 거짓말이라니.

cloze.en: To think the person we were looking for was you!

cloze.sentence: 그 어려운 시험에 한 번에 {{}} 정말 대단하다.
cloze.en: Passing that hard exam on the first try is really impressive.

nearMiss.hint: The present quoted form reacts to what you heard about a future event; for the fact itself: 합격했다니.

cloze.en: To think the kid is already making meals on her own!

nearMiss.hint: Also natural if you are reacting to what someone told you (the quoted -ㄴ/는다니). The cue asks for the bare-stem -다니: 만들다니.

cloze.en: It's midsummer; it's strange that it's this cold.

nuance.situation: 친구가 회사를 그만뒀다는 걸 방금 알고 놀랐어요. (You just found out your friend quit.)

options.why: Bare-stem -다니 voices surprise at the fact.
-다니까 insists on something you said; it doesn't express your surprise (and the form needs -ㄴ-).

nuance.situation: "I can't believe it was all a dream"을 말하려면? (Expressing disbelief.)

options.why: -았/었다니 + evaluation: disbelief at the fact.
-다니까 means "I told you" or "since (someone) said"; it doesn't express disbelief.

nuance: Continuing or repeating the first action leads to a natural result or realization. The main clause is a general truth, prediction, or advice (-게 되다, -(으)ㄹ 거예요, -기도 하다, -(으)ㄹ 수 있다, -기 마련이다). One-off acts don't fit (문을 열다 보면). The main clause is rarely a one-time past result; for a result that already happened, use -다 보니. With adjectives it means "when one is (constantly) …" (바쁘다 보면 연락을 못 할 때도 있다). See also HowtoStudyKorean Lesson 121.

contrasts.note: -다 보니 reports a result that already came about; -다 보면 predicts or generalizes.
-기 마련이다 often closes a -다 보면 sentence: the outcome is only natural.

examples.ko: 매일 조금씩 연습하다 보면 실력이 늘 거예요.
examples.en: If you keep practicing a little every day, you'll improve.

examples.ko: 번역을 하다 보면 원문에 없는 뜻을 덧붙이고 싶은 유혹을 느끼기도 한다.
examples.en: When you translate, you sometimes feel tempted to add meaning that isn't in the original.

cloze.en: Keep on living, and good days will come too.
If you practice a little every day, you'll get better.

nearMiss.hint: -다 보니 reports what already happened; for a prediction or advice use -다 보면.

cloze.sentence: 이 길로 쭉 {{}} 오른쪽에 약국이 보일 거예요.
cloze.en: Keep going down this road and you'll see a pharmacy on the right.

cloze.sentence: 일이 {{}} 연락을 못 할 때도 있지.
cloze.en: When you're busy, there are times you can't keep in touch.

cloze.sentence: 외국에서 오래 {{}} 한국 음식이 그리워질 때가 있어요.
cloze.en: Living abroad a long time, there are times you miss Korean food.

cloze.sentence: 그 사람 얘기를 {{}} 시간 가는 줄 몰라요.
cloze.en: Listening to him talk, you lose track of time.

nearMiss.hint: 듣- keeps ㄷ before a consonant: 듣다 보면.

cloze.en: Work together long enough and you're bound to grow attached.

cloze.sentence: 번역을 {{}} 원문에 없는 뜻을 덧붙이고 싶은 유혹을 느끼기도 한다.
cloze.en: When you translate, you are sometimes tempted to add meaning not in the original.

nuance.situation: 어느 문장이 자연스러워요? (Which sentence is natural?)

options.why: Opening a door is a one-off act; -다 보면 needs an activity that keeps going or repeats.

options.text: 책을 많이 읽다 보면 어휘력이 늘어요.
options.why: Reading is ongoing, and the main clause states the natural outcome.

nuance.situation: 지난 1년 동안 매일 한국 드라마를 봤고, 그래서 귀가 트였어요. 그 결과를 말하려면? (A result that has already happened.)

options.text: 매일 드라마를 보다 보니 귀가 트였어요.
options.why: A result that already came about: -다 보니.

options.text: 매일 드라마를 보다 보면 귀가 트였어요.
options.why: -다 보면 predicts or generalizes; it can't take a past-tense result.

meaning: as (I) kept …, (I found / it turned out that) …; with adjectives and 이다: since (it is constantly) …
nuance: Reports a result or realization that came about by continuing an action (얘기하다 보니 시간이 이렇게 됐네) or from an ongoing circumstance. With adjectives and 이다, it explains a reason rooted in circumstances, softer and more explanatory than -아/어서 (집이 멀다 보니 자주 못 와요; 주말이다 보니 사람이 많네요). The main clause is past or a present state, not a command, suggestion, or plan. See also HowtoStudyKorean Lesson 122.

contrasts.note: -다 보면 predicts or generalizes; -다 보니 reports what has already come about.
-아/어 보니(까) is discovery from one deliberate try; -다 보니 is through repetition or circumstance.

meaning: having tried / actually done …, (I found that) …
nuance: 보다 here means "try, experience". The first action is a deliberate check or first experience, and the main clause is what the speaker discovered, often contrary to expectations: 막상 해 보니 어렵지 않았다. Words like 막상, 직접, 실제로 often appear. The discoverer is the speaker. Compare -았/었더니 (my action, then a result or reaction, not necessarily a test) and -다 보니 (discovery through repetition over time). See also HowtoStudyKorean Lesson 123.

contrasts.note: -았/었더니 covers results and reactions to anything you did; -아/어 보니 frames the act as a try or check.
-다 보니 = through doing it over and over; -아/어 보니 = after one try.

meaning: (1) worth …-ing; (2) good enough to …, bearable, decent; (3) (with 도) understandable that …
nuance: Three readings: worth it (가 볼 만한 곳, 주목할 만한 결과), passable or manageable (참을 만하다, 먹을 만해요 = "it's fine, edible" — lukewarm, not high praise), and understandable, usually with 도 (화가 날 만도 하다). It always takes the prospective modifier -(으)ㄹ. Spacing: 볼 만하다 is the base form, and 볼만하다 is also permitted (auxiliary attachment). ㄹ-stems: 들 만하다 (from 들다) vs 들을 만하다 (from 듣다). See also HowtoStudyKorean Lesson 124.

contrasts.note: -는 편이다 hedges a tendency; -(으)ㄹ 만하다 rates something as worth it or acceptable.
-기 마련이다 says something is bound to happen; -(으)ㄹ 만도 하다 says it is understandable.

nuance.situation: "그 사람이 화낸 것도 이해가 돼요"를 한 문장으로? (It's understandable that they got angry.)

-(으)ㄹ 만큼 means "to the extent that" and needs something to measure; it doesn't mean "understandable".

meaning: I told you …; I'm telling you … (insisting on or repeating what one already said)
nuance: A contraction of -ㄴ/는다고 하니까, used at the end of a sentence to repeat your own earlier statement with impatience or emphasis ("I said I'm fine!"). It follows the quoted form: verbs -ㄴ/는다니까, adjectives -다니까, 이다 -(이)라니까, commands -(으)라니까, suggestions -자니까. 해요체 adds 요. To superiors it can sound pushy; 글쎄 or 정말 often come with it. Mid-sentence, -ㄴ/는다니까 means "when (I/they) said …" (간다니까 좋아하더라). See also HowtoStudyKorean Lesson 125.

contrasts.note: -다니 voices surprise at a fact; -다니까 insists on what you said.
-ㄴ/는다니(요) echoes someone else's words in surprise; -ㄴ/는다니까(요) repeats your own.

meaning: do … (and leave it that way); do … in advance (the result stays in place)
nuance: Completes an action and leaves its result in place: 문을 열어 놓다 (and leave it open), 미리 예약해 놓다. Spoken contractions: 놔(요), 놨다. Often interchangeable with -아/어 두다, but 놓다 is the natural choice for leaving a mess or a state behind (어질러 놓다, 켜 놓고 나가다). -아/어 놓고(서) often carries reproach: did X and then (inconsiderately) … (약속해 놓고 안 왔다). For keeping something for later, 두다 is the more usual collocation (알아 두다, 기억해 두다). See also HowtoStudyKorean Lesson 128.

contrasts.note: -아/어 두다 leans toward storing or keeping for later; -아/어 놓다 toward leaving a result in place, including messes.
-(으)ㄴ 채로 describes doing something while a state lasts; -아/어 놓다 is putting that state in place.

nuance.situation: "어제 숙제를 미리 다 했다. 그래서 오늘은 여유가 있다"를 한 문장으로. (Combine into one sentence.)

options.text: 어제 숙제를 미리 다 해 놔서 오늘은 여유가 있어요.

meaning: do … for later; do … and keep it so (storing a result for future use)
nuance: Like -아/어 놓다, the result remains, but 두다 leans toward keeping or storing it for later use: 알아 두다, 기억해 두다, 저장해 두다, 보관해 두다, 비워 두다, 아껴 두다. Contractions: 둬(요), 뒀다 (from 두어, 두었다). In formal writing, 밝혀 두다 / 말해 두다 put something on record. The reproachful "did X and then …" sense is more typical of -아/어 놓고. See also HowtoStudyKorean Lesson 128.

contrasts.note: -아/어 놓다 stresses leaving the result in place (even a mess); -아/어 두다 stresses keeping it for later.
-아/어 버리다 adds finality or relief or regret; -아/어 두다 keeps something for later use.
